items.question_text: A 79-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer disease is admitted with a displaced neck of femur. She can tell you the operation is to fix the broken hip, name the main risks she has just been told, and say she wants the surgery so she can walk. She cannot recall the name of the hospital or the day of the week. Her son says he has enduring power of attorney and the operation cannot proceed without his signature. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. A dementia diagnosis does not remove it. Assess this decision. If she understands, retains, weighs and communicates it, she can consent. What is the most appropriate next step?  Orientation to day and place is not the capacity test. The son's document is for when she cannot decide. She can decide this operation. Assess and proceed on her consent.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.
options: Assess this decision. If she understands, retains, weighs and communicates it, she can consent
Refuse surgery until the son signs, because dementia removes capacity
Ask the son to consent as substitute decision-maker for every treatment
Sedate her and proceed under a doctrine of necessity without discussion
Delay surgery for a tribunal hearing before any consent
items.subtopic: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. A dementia diagnosis does not remove it.
items.lo_title: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
Capacity is the ability to understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate a decision. It is assessed for this decision at this time. Orientation to day and place is not the test. A diagnosis of dementia does not automatically remove capacity. An enduring power of attorney is used when the person lacks capacity, not instead of her.

B. Refuse surgery until the son signs, because dementia removes capacity
The diagnosis is not the test.

A. Assess this decision. If she understands, retains, weighs and communicates it, she can consent
This is the correct step.

C. Ask the son to consent as substitute decision-maker for every treatment
He is not the decision-maker while she has capacity for this choice.

D. Sedate her and proceed under a doctrine of necessity without discussion
She is engaging with the decision. Necessity is not a shortcut around a capacious refusal or consent.

E. Delay surgery for a tribunal hearing before any consent
A tribunal is for unresolved disputes or a need for a formal appointment, not the first step here.
items.diagnosis_explanation: She can engage with this operation. Dementia and a son's power of attorney do not replace her consent.
key_takeaways: Capacity is decision-specific.
An enduring power of attorney operates when capacity is lacking.

items.question_text: A 54-year-old man with a bleeding duodenal ulcer understands that without endoscopic therapy he may die. He can repeat the risks, says he has weighed them, and refuses the procedure for reasons he can explain. He is not intoxicated or delirious. His wife insists you proceed and says she will sign the form. A capacious refusal of treatment stands, even if the family and the clinician disagree. Respect the refusal, document the capacity assessment, and explain the risk again. What is the most appropriate course?  Emergency doctrine is for the person who cannot consent, not the person who has refused. His wife cannot override him. Document and respect the refusal.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.
options: Proceed. A spouse can override a refusal of life-saving treatment
Respect the refusal, document the capacity assessment, and explain the risk again
Sedate him. Emergency doctrine allows treatment over any refusal
Ask hospital security to hold him so the endoscopist can start
Treat the refusal as attempted suicide and schedule him under a mental health order
items.subtopic: A capacious refusal of treatment stands, even if the family and the clinician disagree.
items.lo_title: A capacious refusal of treatment stands

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
A competent adult may refuse treatment, including life-saving treatment. The family's wish does not override that refusal. Emergency treatment without consent is for a person who cannot consent, not for a person who has refused.

A. Proceed. A spouse can override a refusal of life-saving treatment
She cannot.

B. Respect the refusal, document the capacity assessment, and explain the risk again
This is the course.

C. Sedate him. Emergency doctrine allows treatment over any refusal
Emergency doctrine is not a way past a capacious refusal.

D. Ask hospital security to hold him so the endoscopist can start
That is restraint to force treatment on a capacious adult.

E. Treat the refusal as attempted suicide and schedule him under a mental health order
Refusal of treatment is not, by itself, a mental illness or a reason for involuntary care.
items.diagnosis_explanation: He has capacity and has refused. His wife cannot sign him into the procedure.
key_takeaways: A capacious refusal stands.
Emergency treatment is for the person who cannot consent, not the person who refuses.

items.question_text: A 28-year-old is brought in unconscious after a high-speed crash. He has a rigid abdomen and hypotension. No family is present. A laparotomy is needed now. A colleague says you must wait for a relative to sign. Emergency treatment can proceed without consent when the person cannot consent and delay would cause serious harm. Proceed with life-saving surgery. What is the most appropriate action?  Waiting for a signature may kill him. Staff cannot consent on his behalf. A tribunal cannot move at this speed. Operate.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.
options: Wait for the next of kin. No operation without a signature
Apply to a tribunal before the first incision
Proceed with life-saving surgery. He cannot consent and delay risks death
Ask two nurses to sign as substitute decision-makers
Give blood only. Surgery needs written consent even in cardiac arrest
items.subtopic: Emergency treatment can proceed without consent when the person cannot consent and delay would cause serious harm.
items.lo_title: Emergency treatment without consent when the person cannot consent

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
If a person lacks capacity and treatment is needed at once to prevent serious harm, it may be given in their best interests. Waiting for a signature is not required and may be harmful.

A. Wait for the next of kin. No operation without a signature
Delay for a signature is the error.

C. Proceed with life-saving surgery. He cannot consent and delay risks death
This is the action.

B. Apply to a tribunal before the first incision
A tribunal cannot move at the speed of uncontrolled bleeding.

D. Ask two nurses to sign as substitute decision-makers
Staff signatures are not a substitute consent.

E. Give blood only. Surgery needs written consent even in cardiac arrest
The same emergency principle covers the operation.
items.diagnosis_explanation: He cannot consent and he will die if you wait. Proceed.
key_takeaways: Emergency treatment does not wait for a signature.
Staff cannot consent on a patient's behalf.

items.question_text: A 15-year-old girl asks for a prescription for the oral contraceptive pill. Age under 16 is not an absolute bar. Competence for this decision brings confidentiality with it. Do not phone her parents as the first step.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.
options: Refuse. No one under 16 can consent to any treatment
Phone her parents and proceed only with their consent
Supply the pill but tell the parents, because confidentiality does not apply under 16
Assess her understanding. If she is competent for this decision, she may consent
Refer her to a court before any contraceptive advice

items.lo_title: A mature minor may consent if Gillick competent

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
A minor who can understand the nature and consequences of the decision may consent to it. Age under 16 is not an absolute bar. Confidentiality follows that competence, unless a risk threshold is crossed.

A. Refuse. No one under 16 can consent to any treatment
Competence, not a fixed age, is the test.

D. Assess her understanding. If she is competent for this decision, she may consent
This is the course.

B. Phone her parents and proceed only with their consent
Competent minors are not automatically overruled by parents.

C. Supply the pill but tell the parents, because confidentiality does not apply under 16
Competence brings confidentiality with it.

E. Refer her to a court before any contraceptive advice
Ordinary contraceptive care does not need a court.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Assess this 15-year-old for this decision. Age alone does not block consent.
key_takeaways: Gillick competence is decision-specific.
A competent minor's confidentiality is respected.

items.question_text: A 32-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. He is well. He asks that his wife not be told. He says he will keep having unprotected sex with her and will not tell her himself. Confidentiality may be breached to prevent a serious, identifiable risk. It is not breached for family curiosity. Urge him to tell her. If he will not, disclosure to protect her may be justified. What is the most appropriate course?  She is a named person at serious risk. Urge disclosure first. If he refuses, limited disclosure to protect her may be justified. Absolute secrecy does not hold.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.
options: Keep absolute confidentiality. A spouse has no right to this information
Tell his employer first, then his wife
Enter the diagnosis on My Health Record without discussion
Refuse all further care until he signs a disclosure form
Urge him to tell her. If he will not, disclosure to protect her may be justified

items.lo_title: Confidentiality may be breached to prevent serious identifiable harm

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
Confidentiality is not absolute. A serious, identifiable risk to a named person can justify disclosure after the person has been urged to tell and has refused. The disclosure is limited to what that person needs.

A. Keep absolute confidentiality. A spouse has no right to this information
Absolute confidentiality does not hold where she is at serious risk.

E. Urge him to tell her. If he will not, disclosure to protect her may be justified
This is the course.

B. Tell his employer first, then his wife
The employer is not the person at risk.

C. Enter the diagnosis on My Health Record without discussion
That is not the protective disclosure, and it is not a substitute for the duty.

D. Refuse all further care until he signs a disclosure form
Care continues. The disclosure decision is separate.
items.diagnosis_explanation: She is a named person at serious risk. Urge him to tell her, then consider limited disclosure.
key_takeaways: Confidentiality yields to a serious identifiable risk.
Urge disclosure first. Limit what is shared.

items.question_text: A 13-year-old boy tells you his stepfather hits him with a belt and he is frightened to go home. He asks you to promise not to tell anyone. There are bruises of different ages on his back. A child's confidence is not a reason to hide abuse. Mandatory reporting overrides that promise. Explain you cannot keep this secret, ensure his safety, and make the required report. What is the most appropriate action?  Do not promise secrecy. Do not alert the stepfather first. Protect him and report. Documentation alone is not enough.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.
options: Explain you cannot keep this secret, ensure his safety, and make the required report
Keep the promise. A child's request for secrecy is absolute
Tell the stepfather so he can explain
Wait until the boy turns 16, then report
Document the bruises and take no other action if the boy refuses an examination
items.subtopic: A child's confidence is not a reason to hide abuse. Mandatory reporting overrides that promise.
items.lo_title: Mandatory reporting of child abuse overrides confidentiality

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
A disclosure and injuries of this kind raise suspected child abuse. The duty to report and to protect overrides a promise of secrecy. The child should be told, in terms he can understand, that you cannot keep this secret.

B. Keep the promise. A child's request for secrecy is absolute
It is not, where he may be at risk of harm.

A. Explain you cannot keep this secret, ensure his safety, and make the required report
This is the action.

C. Tell the stepfather so he can explain

D. Wait until the boy turns 16, then report
The duty is present now.

E. Document the bruises and take no other action if the boy refuses an examination
Documentation without protection and reporting is not enough.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Do not promise secrecy. Protect him and report.
key_takeaways: Suspected child abuse is reported.
A promise of secrecy does not override that duty.

items.question_text: A woman has consented to a diagnostic laparoscopy for pelvic pain. At operation the surgeon finds an uncomplicated ovarian cyst and removes the ovary, believing she would have wanted it done. She had not discussed oophorectomy. Consent for a procedure covers that procedure. It does not silently cover an unrelated extra. Removing the ovary without discussion exceeded the consent. What is the most appropriate judgment?  The cyst was not life-threatening on the table. Extra surgery needs its own consent, or true emergency necessity. This exceeded the consent. The form is not a blank cheque.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.
options: Consent to laparoscopy includes any related organ removal
Removing the ovary without discussion exceeded the consent
A finding at operation always authorises extra surgery
The consent form signature covers whatever the surgeon later thinks best
Battery applies only if the original procedure was also unconsented
items.subtopic: Consent for a procedure covers that procedure. It does not silently cover an unrelated extra.
items.lo_title: Consent covers the procedure discussed, not silent extras

blueprint.note: Coverage reporting and tie-break only. Not a quota.

items.explanation:
Consent is for the procedure discussed. An extra procedure that was not needed to save life or prevent serious immediate harm, and was not agreed, is outside that consent.

A. Consent to laparoscopy includes any related organ removal
Related does not mean any additional operation.

B. Removing the ovary without discussion exceeded the consent
This is the judgment.

C. A finding at operation always authorises extra surgery

D. The consent form signature covers whatever the surgeon later thinks best
The form records the discussion. It is not a blank cheque.

E. Battery applies only if the original procedure was also unconsented
An unconsented extra procedure can itself be a battery.
items.diagnosis_explanation: The cyst removal was not the operation she agreed to, and it was not an emergency.
key_takeaways: Consent is procedure-specific.

What is the most appropriate course?  Mild cognitive impairment is not incapacity. He understands this colonoscopy. The daughter's refusal does not transfer the decision. Take his consent.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.

Split the difference and book a CT instead, without asking him
Take his consent. The power of attorney is not active while he has capacity

items.explanation:

A. Follow the daughter. An enduring power of attorney always outranks the patient

C. Take his consent. The power of attorney is not active while he has capacity
This is the course.

items.diagnosis_explanation: He can decide. The daughter's document does not silence him.

Genetic risk is not an automatic breach.  The facts already in front of you are enough to decide. Do not add a step the law does not require.  Capacity, consent, and confidentiality are decided on this person and this decision, not on a relative's wish or a form. Apply that rule here.  Nothing further in the history changes the duty in front of you.  Decide on the information already given. A further signature or a family demand does not change it. Apply it.

Write the result to the sister's GP without telling your patient
Refuse to give your patient the result until she agrees to tell her family
Encourage her to tell her sister. Do not disclose now in the absence of an imminent serious harm
